headline: The Taxpayer First Act, signed in 2019, changes how the IRS handles customer service, collections, appeals, identity theft, and technology.
what_it_does: The law creates an independent IRS appeals office to settle tax disputes without going to court. It limits some IRS collection tools, such as seizing property and sending tax debts to private collectors, and adds protections for certain taxpayers. It also requires the IRS to improve identity theft protection, electronic filing, and information technology, and it sets new rules for tax return preparers and tax-exempt groups. Several provisions require Treasury or the IRS to send reports, plans, or notices to Congress or taxpayers.

who_it_affects.how: They can have their disputes reviewed by a new Independent Office of Appeals, which aims to resolve cases without litigation.

They are exempt from paying a user fee with an offer-in-compromise and are excluded from referrals of tax debts to private collection agencies, and they can get help from volunteer tax assistance programs and low-income taxpayer clinics.
Their tax debts cannot be referred to private debt collection agencies.

who_it_affects.group: Taxpayers with tax debts sent to private collectors
who_it_affects.how: Their installment agreements can now run up to seven years instead of five.
They get a single IRS contact point, notice of suspected identity theft, and an identity protection number program.
They face higher civil and criminal penalties for improper disclosure or use of taxpayer information.
They must file their returns electronically and receive notice from the IRS before their tax-exempt status is revoked for failure to file.

who_it_affects.group: Taxpayers who fail to file a return
who_it_affects.how: They face a higher monetary penalty for failure to file.

who_it_affects.group: Former IRS employees fired for misconduct
who_it_affects.how: The IRS may not rehire them.
The IRS may share certain return information with them related to investigations they helped with.

who_it_affects.group: People who pay taxes by debit or credit card
who_it_affects.how: The IRS must recoup card processing fees charged by card companies for these payments.

who_it_affects.group: People who use the IRS e-Services tools
who_it_affects.how: They must have their identity verified before opening an e-Services account.

when_it_takes_effect: Provisions take effect on various dates set in the law, with some tied to 2020 deadlines and the Form 1099 internet platform due by January 1, 2023; the enactment date was July 1, 2019.
